title: Wren's Wobbly Dreams
markdown:
Wren the rabbit lived in a little burrow, warm and safe beneath the whispering willow. Moss made carpets on the floor. The air smelled of dry earth and sweet clover. Beside her, on a cushion that looked as if it had been woven from moonlight, sat Teacup the teddy bear. Teacup’s fur was cloud-soft. His button eyes held a kind of quiet understanding, and his stitched smile always seemed ready to comfort. Wren loved that burrow with all her bunny heart. She loved the way moonlight laid dancing patterns on the moss. She loved her special shelf of smoothest, prettiest pebbles.

Tonight, though, as the last pale light melted into a big dark sky, a flutter started in Wren’s chest. Her whiskers twitched. Her dreams, which usually felt like warm flowing streams, seemed all crumpled, like a drawing squeezed into a tight ball. If her dreams stayed crumpled, she would wake up grumpy, and she did not want to be grumpy for the morning’s fun. Her ears drooped. A tiny sighing breath escaped her.

Oh, Teacup, she whispered, as soft as petals falling. My dreams are all jumbled. They don’t feel quite right, and my tummy feels a little wiggly.

Teacup, in his special quiet way, gave a slow, comforting squeeze of his paw. He knew what Wren needed. Sometimes dreams wanted smoothing, the way a favorite blanket wanted smoothing when it had gone all wrinkled. They needed the Dream Laundry, a quiet place past the sleepy fields, where dreams were made smooth again for sleeping. The moon was already climbing. If they lingered, the best quiet dream hours would slip away, and Wren’s wobbly feelings might keep her too restless for sleep. She might even miss chasing butterflies in the morning.

Wren nudged Teacup with her nose. Come, Teacup, she said, brighter now, but still as soft as a secret. We must go to the Dream Laundry. We must make my dreams smooth again.

They hopped out into twilight that smelled of clover kissed by dew and of damp, welcoming earth. The path shimmered faintly with moon-dust and led them from their safe home into hushed woods. Trees stood like sleeping giants. Leaves rustled secrets to the evening breeze. Wren’s paws felt less sure on the moss. For a moment she imagined the shadows holding funny wiggly shapes, and she held Teacup a little closer. Nothing chased them. Still, the woods were a little new, and new things made her whiskers tremble until Teacup’s stitched paw squeezed hers again.

The air grew warmer as they walked, filled with a musical humming, as if crickets were singing lullabies in their sleep. Flowers along the verge glowed as softly as banked coals. At last they came to a little cottage nestled among those flowers. Its windows shone amber. Warmth leaked from the door-crack, and it smelled of soap and sleep. This was the Dream Laundry.

Inside, shelves ran all around, crowded with shiny delicate bottles. In each bottle a dream swirled in gentle colors: soft blues, peaceful purples, warm yellows, waiting to be made perfect. A kind old rabbit named Weaver, with wise eyes and a soft apron stitched with tiny sleepy stars, smiled at them. Welcome, little ones, she whispered. What sweet dreams can I help you with today.

Wren pointed, a little nervously, to a bottle of blues and violets. In the middle sat a cloudy smudged patch, as if a bit of worry had settled there. It looked just like her own crumpled dreams. Her whiskers drooped again. She wanted to hop straight home and pretend the crumples were not there. The smudge felt too much like her wobbly feelings, and it made her want to hide.

Weaver saw the worry in Wren’s bright eyes. Ah, a little smudged dream, she said, her voice like a warm hug. We can smooth that right out. Even dreams need a gentle touch now and then.

She took the bottle carefully and set it on a gentle machine that hummed like a contented cat. Warm light threw dancing patterns on the floor, like fireflies playing tag. Other bottles on the shelves turned a slow inch, as if they were listening. Wren watched, Teacup held close, his familiar softness against her fur. It was a quiet waiting, a held breath, a stillness between one thought and the next. She did not snatch the bottle back. She let it sit, even though the smudge still felt like her own, and she counted the hums the way she sometimes counted raindrops on the burrow roof.

Her paws trembled just a tiny bit. Weaver’s kind eyes met hers, and Wren nodded. From her little pouch she drew her favorite perfectly smooth grey pebble, cool and calming in her fur, and placed it in Weaver’s hand. It smelled faintly of dried clover. The machine hummed. A gentle warmth wrapped pebble and bottle together. Giving up the pebble for a moment felt like a small brave thing, and she knew it was needed.

Weaver lifted the bottle into the warm light and turned it slowly. The smudge was gone. Blues and violets swirled as clear as a quiet lake at dawn. Wren peered in and saw a calm sky with no clouds at all. Her crumpled dream was smooth and beautiful, ready for a night of peaceful sleep. Her heart felt light as a dandelion seed. She nuzzled Weaver’s apron in thanks.

Back in the burrow, moonlight painted silver stripes across the moss. Wren and Teacup snuggled down. Wren closed her eyes and, instead of crumpled paper, saw a vast star-filled sky, just like the dream Weaver had smoothed, full of gentle wonder.

A little later the willow rustled lullabies outside. Wren stirred. A faint echo of the old worry brushed her, a whisper of the smudge. Then she remembered Weaver and the Dream Laundry and the clear, beautiful dream. With a soft sigh she nestled deeper, Teacup a warm comforting weight beside her. And as she slept, moonlight and clover filled her dreams, as soft and peaceful as the night itself.
